Relationship Between Swimming and Running Performance in Triathletes¶

Authors: Elena Liaño Rengel and Varvara Gkiouzepa Petropoulou

Public project website: GitHub Pages: https://elenaliano.github.io/

Course: CMPS3160 - Intro to Data Science

Project Description and Research Questions¶

This project focuses on the relationship between swimming and running performance in triathlon. More specifically, whether athletes who perform well in swimming also tend to perform well in running, and if this relationship differs across gender and age groups.

To do this, we will work with two different datasets.

Dataset 1 | IRONMAN 70.3 (2004–2020): This dataset contains individual race results from half-distance IRONMAN competitions. It includes competition information, swimming, cycling, and running split times, and also athlete characteristics such as gender and age group.

Dataset 2 | Multi-Sport Race Result Data: This dataset contains results from different triathlon formats. We select 12 full-distance editions, 6 Olympic-distance editions, and 6 sprint-distance editions. The files include race metadata, split/finish times, gender, and available age information. The professional status variable is not consistently available for the shorter races.

Research questions:

  • To what extent is swimming performance associated with running performance among triathletes?

  • Does the relationship between swimming and running performance vary across age groups, gender (male or female), and competitive status (professionals or amateurs) within triathletes?

  • Does the strength of the association between swimming and running performance differ across triathlon race distances?

  • Do athletes tend to exhibit more balanced swimming and running performances in shorter or longer triathlon events?

This project is significant to us since we are athletes in running and swimming respectively. We are interested to see the results of the correlation of both sports performance and hopefully apply them to our training.

Collaboration Plan¶

The team plan is to meet once a week or as needed to evaluate progress, work on research questions, and resolve problems. Google Drive is used to have a shared space for the team's documents, and Google Colab to write and run Python code. The most common form of communication will be WhatsApp.

We will be dividing the work based on each Milestone's requirements while considering the stronger aspects of each team member. We both worked on the data collection. Our preference is to work in person when deciding on roles and make sure we are communicating ideas freely while discussing our options. We will be using our shared Drive folder to include any drafts and ideas.

1.2. Transform: Cleaning and Reorganizing the Data¶






















We will do some transformation to our table according to tidy data.


We want to rename our columns in a way that it will be easier for reading and understanding. For the variables measured in seconds, SwimTime, Transition1Time, BikeTime, Transition2Time, RunTime, FinishTime, we will exclude the keyword time for space purposes.


















In [ ]:






column_names = {
    "Gender": "Gender",
    "AgeGroup": "Age_Group",
    "AgeBand": "Age_Band",
    "Country": "Country",
    "CountryISO2": "Country_Code",
    "EventYear": "Year",
    "EventLocation": "Event",
    "SwimTime": "Swim",
    "Transition1Time": "Transition_1",
    "BikeTime": "Bike",
    "Transition2Time": "Transition_2",
    "RunTime": "Run",
    "FinishTime": "Finish"
}

df = df_raw.rename(columns=column_names).copy()

df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].replace({
    "M": "Male",
    "F": "Female"
})

df["Event"] = (
    df["Event"]
    .str.replace(r"(?i)^IRONMAN 70\.3\s*", "", regex=True)
    .str.strip(" -,:")
)

























In order for our data sets to be more readable, we also notice that "IRONMAN 70.3" is part of 'Event' for each row, so we strip it. Since this dataset only includes Ironman 70.3, we are more interested in seeing the place of the event or if it is a world champioship or not.


Moreover, we sort the values according to event and year so that it is easier to manipulate.






















Age Group Cleaning and Transformation¶
In this part, we focus on the Age_Group column. Since this variable contains age intervals stored as strings, we can't use it directly in numerical calculations. Additionally, some observations have an age group of "00", which identifies professional athletes. We wanted to address both issues.


First, we created a Boolean column, Is_Pro, to identify professional athletes. Then, we created a new column called Age_Group_Mean by calculating the midpoint of each age interval. For example, athletes in the 30–34 age group are assigned a value of 32. This gives us a numerical representation of the age groups that can be used more easily in calculations and visualizations. For professional athletes, we replaced the resulting zero values with NaN, since we do not know their ages.


Finally, we placed Age_Group_Mean next to Age_Group and removed Age_Band, because it's not necessary for our analysis.


We recognize that Age_Group_Mean does not represent the actual or average age of the athletes within each group, but we will use it as midpoint of their age interval. For that reason, we decided to keep the original Age_Group column to also preserve the original information.


















In [ ]:






df["Is_Pro"] = df["Age_Group"] == "00" # Identify professional athletes

df["Age_Group_Mean"] = (
    df["Age_Group"]
    .str.split("-", expand=True)[[0, 1]]
    .astype(float)
    .mean(axis=1)
    .round()
    .astype("float")
)

df["Age_Group_Mean"] = df["Age_Group_Mean"].replace(0, np.nan)

df.insert(
    df.columns.get_loc("Age_Group") + 1,
    "Age_Group_Mean",
    df.pop("Age_Group_Mean")
)

df = df.drop(columns=["Age_Band"])

display(df[["Age_Group", "Age_Group_Mean"]].head(10))

1.3 Validate: Checking Data Quality¶






















Data Validation and Duplicate Handling¶
We also checked the dataset for missing values, non-positive race times, and duplicate observations.


We identified 17 exact duplicate rows and examined them before removing the additional copies. Since the dataset does not contain unique athlete identifiers, we cannot determine with certainty whether these records represent duplicated entries or different athletes with identical recorded characteristics and times.

print((df[time_cols] <= 0).sum()) # We check for invalid times

print("\nDuplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum()) # We check for duplicate rows

display(df[df.duplicated(keep=False)].sort_values( # We inspect the duplicates

))

After comparing the recorded finish times with the sum of the five race splits, we can see how that the vast majority of observations matched exactly, while some showed small differences: between -2 and +4 seconds.


However, we identified one observation from Bintan (2017) with a difference of 846 seconds between the recorded finish time and the sum of the splits, which is considerably larger than the others. Since we can't treat small differences as incorrect recordings, we decided to allow up to 5 seconds differences and exclude any observations exceeding this threshold to avoid including potentially unreliable data in our analysis.






















1.4 Final Dataset¶
After identifying the inconsistencies in our dataset, we can now create the final cleaned table. We will exclude observations whose recorded finish times differ from the sum of their splits by more than 5 seconds, remove exact duplicate rows, and sort the remaining observations by event and year.


















In [ ]:






df_tidy = df[finish_difference.abs() <= 5].copy()

df_tidy = df_tidy.drop_duplicates()

df_tidy = df_tidy.sort_values(
    ["Event", "Year"]
).reset_index(drop=True)

print("Original records:", len(df_raw))
print("Final records:", len(df_tidy))
print("Remaining duplicates:", df_tidy.duplicated().sum())

After applying these cleaning steps, our dataset was reduced from 840,075 to 840,057 observations. In total, we excluded one inconsistent race result and removed 17 exact duplicate rows. However, since the dataset does not contain unique athlete identifiers, we cannot be completely certain that these duplicates represent repeated entries or different athletes with identical recorded information. The final table retains the variables needed for our research questions and is now ready for exploratory data analysis.






















Gender-Based Subsets¶
We will split our data set into two. One set for women and one set for men. Since gender plays a big role in performance, we can compare the relationship in running and swimming for men and women seperately. We also reset the index so that the rows are numbered consecutively. But will keep the complete dataset for our overall analysis.


















In [ ]:






print("Gender categories:", df["Gender"].unique()) #data validation to check gender categories

#We create gender subsets
men_df = df_tidy[df_tidy["Gender"] == "Male"].copy()
women_df = df_tidy[df_tidy["Gender"] == "Female"].copy()

men_df = men_df.reset_index(drop=True)
women_df = women_df.reset_index(drop=True)

print("Men's dataset:", men_df.shape)
print("Women's dataset:", women_df.shape)

display(men_df.head())
display(women_df.head())

1.5 Tidy data justification¶
After cleaning and validating our data, we can evaluate whether our final table follows the principles of tidy data.


Our original dataset was already relatively well structured, so we decided to preserve its overall format while improving consistency and data quality.


The final dataset satisfies the three principles of tidy data:


    

  1. Each variable forms a column. Athlete characteristics (gender, age group, and country), event information (year and location), and performance measurements (swimming, cycling, running, transitions, and finish times) are stored in separate columns.
    

    2. 

  2. Each observation forms a row. Every row represents one athlete's result in a particular IRONMAN 70.3 race.
    

    3. 

  3. Each type of observational unit forms a table. All observations represent individual race results, so there is no need to separate different types of observations into additional tables.
    

    4. 



We also retained both Age_Group and Age_Group_Mean, allowing us to preserve the original age intervals while having a numerical approximation available for analysis.


Finally, although we created separate male and female subsets to facilitate comparisons, we kept the complete dataset as our main tidy table. This allows us to analyze the relationship between swimming and running performance both overall and within each gender group.






















1.6 Challenges and Limitations¶






















Challenges¶
    

  • Unknown exact ages: We only know the athletes' age intervals, not their actual ages.
    

    • 

  • Age Group data type: Age_Group was stored as an object, which made direct numerical calculations difficult.
    

    • 

  • Professional athletes: The value "00" represents professionals but not their age.
    

    • 

  • Duplicate rows: We identified and removed 17 duplicates, although we cannot confirm they represent the same athletes.
    

    • 

  • Inconsistent finish times: One observation had a discrepancy of 846 seconds and was excluded.
    

    • 

  • Gender-based analysis: In our first approach, we split the dataset into men and women first and then applied all the changes which took much more space than intended
    

    • 























2. Dataset 2: Multi-Sport Race Result Data¶

2.1 Extract: Load and Inspect Data¶






















This dataset comes from a publicly available GitHub repository. So we can retrieve its data directly from GitHub using Python.


This approach makes our notebook more accessible and reproducible because anyone running it can obtain the original data. We initially download the complete repository, preserving its original structure.


It contains race results (.tsv) and race metadata (edition.json) for many years and formats. The .tsv files don't use the same columns for all, so we keep the original files in their separate folders.


















In [ ]:






repo_folder = Path("triathlon-result-data")

if not repo_folder.exists():
    subprocess.run([
        "git", "clone", "--depth", "1",
        "https://github.com/matsubo/triathlon-result-data.git", # we download Dataset 2 directly from its GitHub repo
        str(repo_folder)
    ], check=True)

results_folder = repo_folder / "master" # we locate the results and metadata files

result_files = sorted(results_folder.rglob("*.tsv"))
metadata_files = sorted(results_folder.rglob("edition.json"))

print("TSV results files:", len(result_files))
print("Race metadata files:", len(metadata_files))
print("Repository location:", results_folder.resolve())

























TSV results files: 2998
Race metadata files: 2697
Repository location: /content/triathlon-result-data/master

























The output tells us how many result tables and metadata files were found. In our initial download, the repository contained 2,998 TSV result files and 2,697 edition.json files. These numbers are not expected to match: one race edition can include separate result tables for different categories or distances.


Because we download the repository from GitHub, these counts may change if new races are added. We will keep the original file paths so we can trace each observation back to its source






















Exploration of the Dataset¶
For each .tsv, we read its corresponding edition.json and record the race, year, distance category, and official swimming/cycling/running distances. We count its result rows and note the number of columns (keeping the original data unchanged). All this to create a catalog of every result file.


This inventory is going to help us answer: What race distances, years, and competitions are available? Which files have the three splits we need for our four research questions? We will check later split columns and data quality.


















In [ ]:






all_races = [] # we read the metadata for ALL the race results

for file in result_files:
    metadata = json.loads((file.parent / "edition.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    category = next(c for c in metadata["categories"] if c["id"] == file.stem)
    segments = {s["sport"]: s.get("distance") for s in category.get("segments", [])}

    with file.open(encoding="utf-8-sig", errors="replace", newline="") as source: # we inspect the raw TSV structure without changing anything yet
        rows = csv.reader(source, delimiter="\t")
        headers = next(rows, [])
        num_rows = sum(bool(row and any(value.strip() for value in row)) for row in rows)

    all_races.append({
        "Event": file.parent.parent.name,
        "Race_Date": file.parent.name,
        "Year": int(file.parent.name[:4]),
        "Distance_Code": category.get("distance"),
        "Swim_km": segments.get("swim"),
        "Bike_km": segments.get("bike"),
        "Run_km": segments.get("run"),
        "Results": num_rows,
        "Columns": len(headers),
        "File": str(file)
    })

df_catalog = pd.DataFrame(all_races)

print("Total race result files:", len(df_catalog))
print("Total rows across files:", df_catalog["Results"].sum())
display(df_catalog.head(10))

2.2. Cleaning and Reorganizing the Data¶






















Selection of Race Editions for the Main Analysis¶
After inspecting the catalog we organized, we chose races that can help us answer our research questions. For a first comparable sample, we use sprint, Olympic, and full-distance triathlons from several events and years. Our original first dataset, IRONMAN 70.3, can supply the half-distance category.


We make an initial selection, as shown in the following list. Other race editions can be added or substituted once we assess the data quality. We can verify the recorded segment distances directly against the catalog, which will prevents us from treating shortened swims or modified courses as the standard distances of the events.

The output confirms that all 24 selected TSV files exist and that their recorded swimming, cycling, and running distances match the standards we chose. The table is only a preview of the selected events (head(10)). Its Results column still counts raw entries, before any finisher or time-quality checks.


Checking segment distances here is important for our third and fourth research questions because we want to study differences between race formats.






















Rationale for Event Selection¶
After exploring the complete repository, we selected 24 race editions: 6 sprint, 6 Olympic-distance, and 12 full-distance IRONMAN events. Together with our original IRONMAN 70.3 dataset, this gives us four race-distance categories to investigate our research questions.


We based our selection on several factors:


    

  • Race distances: We selected events with standard distances. This allows us to compare the swimming–running relationship in withing different triathlon formats without including races with shortened or modified courses.
    

    • 

  • Different years: We included races from different years (2017, 2019, and 2023) to see whether the relationships are consistent over time. Precisely, we took the 2017 and 2019 results because they overlap with the period covered by our first dataset (2004–2020), and then the 2023 results because they provide more recent observations.
    

    • 

  • Different competitions: We wanted to include multiple races to see if this is a factor to take into account for the correlation between swimming and running performances. In addition, we wanted to represent different geographical locations.
However, we tried to select multiple editions of the same competitions if it was possible, because in that way we can examine if the relationships remained consistent across different years.
    

    • 

  • Data availability and consistency: We prioritized races that contained available swimming and running split times, athlete information, and metadata describing the course distances. Because all these variables are necessary to answer our research questions and combine the results with our original dataset.
    

    • 























2.3 Extract and Inspect¶
The full-distance files have English column names and a regular tab-separated structure. The sprint/Olympic files use Japanese headers (some also contain extra trailing tab fields). We read them carefully, keeping the fields corresponding to the documented headers and checking for extra entries. For the main analysis, we do not need athlete names or the extra trailing fields.

The selected full-distance files contain 29,281 raw results. The preview shows individual athletes and their race information, including Division, Total_Time, Swim, T1, Bike, T2, and Run. At this point, times are still stored as strings, and gender uses M and F.


The Division field is useful because it can distinguish categories such as MPRO and FPRO from age-group competitors. Some rows have an empty Status even when they have a finishing time and rank, so we will not treat a blank status as automatic evidence that an athlete did not finish. We are going to validate completion using several fields together.


















In [ ]:






# some Japanese TSV rows contain extra trailing tabs, so pandas.read_csv() may misalign the columns. That is why we read the fields explicitly
def read_japanese_tsv(file):
    text = Path(file).read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig")
    rows = list(csv.reader(StringIO(text), delimiter="\t"))
    headers = rows[0]
    data = [(row + [""] * len(headers))[:len(headers)] for row in rows[1:]]
    return pd.DataFrame(data, columns=headers)

short_tables = []
for folder, name, date, olympic_file, sprint_file in short_races:
    for file_name, distance in [(olympic_file, "Olympic"), (sprint_file, "Sprint")]:
        file = results_folder / folder / date / file_name
        race = read_japanese_tsv(file)
        race["Event"] = name
        race["Year"] = int(date[:4])
        race["Race_Date"] = date
        race["Race_Distance"] = distance
        race["Source_File"] = str(file.relative_to(results_folder))
        short_tables.append(race)
        print(name, date[:4], distance, "raw results:", len(race))

df_short_raw = pd.concat(short_tables, ignore_index=True)
print("Sprint + Olympic raw records:", len(df_short_raw))
display(df_short_raw.head())

The remaining columns (Event, Year, Race_Date, Race_Distance, and Source_File) are the ones we have added during extraction to identify the competition and its original source.


We will standardize these column names during the transformation stage to make the data easier to work with and compatible with our first dataset.






















2.4 Transform¶
We are going to convert time strings to seconds and standardize gender labels to make them match to the ones of dataset 1. The full-distance files report the transition times T1 and T2 as separate splits. In sprint/Olympic files, only some editions report T1 separately, and in other editions the transition time is included in the broader bike split. So we are going to retain the original swim and run split times for the comparisons and not assume transitions can be compared across sources.


The sprint/Olympic files also report athletes' numerical ages, while the IRONMAN sources mostly use age categories. We are going to preserve the available age information and distinguish exact ages from group midpoints.


















In [ ]:






# Full IRONMAN: standardize times and athlete characteristics.
df_full = df_full_raw.rename(columns={
    "T1": "Transition_1", "T2": "Transition_2", "Total_Time": "Finish"
}).copy()

full_time_cols = ["Swim", "Transition_1", "Bike", "Transition_2", "Run", "Finish"]
for column in full_time_cols:
    df_full[column] = pd.to_timedelta(df_full[column], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds()

df_full["Gender"] = df_full["Gender"].map({"M": "Male", "F": "Female"})
df_full["Overall_Rank"] = pd.to_numeric(df_full["Overall_Rank"], errors="coerce")

division = df_full["Division"].fillna("").str.upper().str.strip()
df_full["Age_Group"] = division.str.extract(r"(\d{2}-\d{2})", expand=False)
df_full.loc[division.isin(["MPRO", "FPRO"]), "Age_Group"] = "00"
age_limits = df_full["Age_Group"].str.extract(r"(\d{2})-(\d{2})")
df_full["Age_Estimate"] = age_limits.astype(float).mean(axis=1)
df_full["Age_Exact"] = np.nan

df_full["Is_Pro"] = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=df_full.index, dtype="boolean")
df_full.loc[division.isin(["MPRO", "FPRO"]), "Is_Pro"] = True
df_full.loc[division.str.match(r"^[MF]\d{2}-\d{2}$"), "Is_Pro"] = False

df_full["Competition_Group"] = df_full["Is_Pro"].map({
    True: "Professional", False: "Age-group"
}).fillna("Not reported")
df_full["Data_Source"] = "Multi-Sport Race Result Data"
df_full["Timing_Convention"] = "Five splits reported separately"

print(df_full[["Event", "Year", "Gender", "Age_Group", "Is_Pro", "Swim", "Run", "Finish"]].dtypes)
display(df_full[["Event", "Year", "Gender", "Age_Group", "Is_Pro", "Swim", "Run", "Finish"]].head())

The displayed dtypes confirm that split times and finishing times are now numeric (float64). All times are measured in seconds, which will let us calculate correlations and compare variables with Dataset 1.


The preview also shows how we standardized gender and used Division to identify professional athletes where the source explicitly reports them. Age_Group = "00" is a code for the professional division, not an actual age. We keep exact age missing for these records.


















In [ ]:






# Sprint/Olympic: different Japanese spellings of the same columns
def first_column(frame, candidates):
    return next((name for name in candidates if name in frame.columns), None)

short_cleaned = []
for race in short_tables:
    swim_col = first_column(race, ["スイムラップ", "ｽｲﾑﾗｯﾌﾟ"])
    bike_col = first_column(race, ["バイクラップ", "ﾊﾞｲｸﾗｯﾌﾟ"])
    run_col = first_column(race, ["ランラップ", "ﾗﾝﾗｯﾌﾟ"])
    age_group_col = first_column(race, ["年齢区分", "年代区分", "区分"])
    assert all([swim_col, bike_col, run_col]), race["Source_File"].iloc[0]

    age = pd.to_numeric(race["年齢"], errors="coerce")
    cleaned = pd.DataFrame({
        "Event": race["Event"], "Year": race["Year"],
        "Race_Date": race["Race_Date"], "Race_Distance": race["Race_Distance"],
        "Source_File": race["Source_File"],
        "Data_Source": "Multi-Sport Race Result Data",
        "Gender": race["性別"].map({"男": "Male", "女": "Female", "M": "Male", "F": "Female"}),
        "Age_Exact": age,
        "Original_Age_Category": race[age_group_col] if age_group_col else pd.NA,
        "Overall_Rank": pd.to_numeric(race["総合順位"], errors="coerce"),
        "Swim": pd.to_timedelta(race[swim_col], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds(),
        "Bike": pd.to_timedelta(race[bike_col], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds(),
        "Run": pd.to_timedelta(race[run_col], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds(),
        "Finish": pd.to_timedelta(race["総合記録"], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds()
    })

    # Some editions have a measured T1; none of these 12 files has a separate T2.
    cleaned["Transition_1"] = (
        pd.to_timedelta(race["T1"], errors="coerce").dt.total_seconds()
        if "T1" in race.columns else np.nan
    )
    cleaned["T1_Reported"] = "T1" in race.columns
    cleaned["Transition_2"] = np.nan
    cleaned["Is_Pro"] = pd.Series(pd.NA, index=race.index, dtype="boolean")
    cleaned["Competition_Group"] = "Not reported"
    cleaned["Age_Estimate"] = age

    # Use exact age to make five-year age bands compatible with Dataset 1.
    lower_age = (age // 5 * 5)
    cleaned["Age_Group"] = lower_age.map(
        lambda n: f"{int(n):02d}-{int(n+4):02d}" if pd.notna(n) else pd.NA
    )
    cleaned["Timing_Convention"] = (
        "T1 separately reported; T2 not separately reported"
        if "T1" in race.columns else
        "Neither transition separately reported"
    )
    short_cleaned.append(cleaned)

df_short = pd.concat(short_cleaned, ignore_index=True)
print("Sprint/Olympic original categories and standardized age bands:")
display(df_short[["Event", "Year", "Original_Age_Category", "Age_Exact", "Age_Group"]].head())
print(df_short[["Swim", "Transition_1", "Bike", "Transition_2", "Run", "Finish"]].dtypes)

Here we keep each athlete's exact age when it is available and we create a common five-year Age_Group for comparisons.


All race times now have numeric types. However, they still can contain missing values: Transition_1 is missing when that edition did not report it, and none of these selected Japanese files report Transition_2 separately. The data also does not identify professionals, so we leave Is_Pro unknown.






















Investigating Missing Transition Times¶
We want to test whether the reported sport splits and any separately reported T1 already account for the total finishing time. When T1 is absent, it is omitted only from the sum, not stored as zero in our cleaned table.


If the recorded split total matches Finish, that tells us the recorded splits account for the race duration. It does not prove T2 was zero, but also does not tell us which sport split includes the missing transition time. For this reason, we retain Transition_2 as missing for Japanese races and flag their different timing conventions.


















In [ ]:






# Investigate the Japanese timing convention by event, year, and distance.
transition_check = df_short[[
    "Event", "Year", "Race_Distance", "Swim", "Transition_1", "Bike", "Run", "Finish"
]].copy()

transition_check["Calculated_Finish"] = (
    transition_check["Swim"] + transition_check["Transition_1"].fillna(0)
    + transition_check["Bike"] + transition_check["Run"]
)
transition_check["Difference"] = (
    transition_check["Finish"] - transition_check["Calculated_Finish"]
)

print("Examples of original and calculated finishing times:")
display(transition_check.head(10))

# Count records whose recorded splits match the finish within five seconds.
transition_summary = transition_check.groupby(
    ["Event", "Year", "Race_Distance"]
)["Difference"].agg(
    Records_Checked="count",
    Matching_Within_5s=lambda x: (x.abs() <= 5).sum(),
    Max_Abs_Difference=lambda x: x.abs().max()
)

display(transition_summary)

Calculated_Finish is the sum of the recorded sport splits and any separately reported T1. In the Difference column we calculate Finish - Calculated_Finish. A value of zero means the recorded values already account for the full finishing time. In the race-level table, Records_Checked counts rows with a calculable difference, Matching_Within_5s counts close matches, and Max_Abs_Difference shows the largest discrepancy.


Most selected Japanese editions match within five seconds. However, in Yokohama Sprint 2017, only 166 of 264 checked records match, and Yokohama Olympic 2023 has one non-matching record out of 1,002. These discrepancies justify why we need to check totals before including observations in our analysis.


A matching total does not show that T2 took zero seconds. It may have been included in another reported split, so we cannot recover an independent T2 value from these data. We will keep that field missing and we will have to point out the limitation that the Japanese running split does not follow exactly the same timing convention as every IRONMAN result






















2.5 Validate and Clean¶
We keep finished results with a valid rank and gender, positive times for all three sports and the overall finish, and a total-time difference no greater than five seconds (as we exactly did in the first dataset). The full-distance files also report both transitions separately; the shorter races do not, so those missing values are not a reason to reject an otherwise valid result.


We preserve the raw tables separately and create new *_tidy DataFrames after filtering. Our resulting sample represents complete finishers, not every registered athlete.


















In [ ]:






# Validate full-distance races (five separately reported splits)
full_diff = df_full["Finish"] - df_full[
    ["Swim", "Transition_1", "Bike", "Transition_2", "Run"]
].sum(axis=1, min_count=5)

status_ok = df_full["Status"].fillna("").str.strip().str.upper().isin(["", "FIN"])
full_valid = (
    status_ok
    & (df_full["Overall_Rank"] > 0)
    & (df_full[full_time_cols] > 0).all(axis=1)
    & df_full["Gender"].isin(["Male", "Female"])
    & (full_diff.abs() <= 5)
)
df_full_tidy = df_full.loc[full_valid].drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

# Validate sprint/Olympic races (transition columns may be missing)
short_diff = transition_check["Difference"]
short_valid = (
    (df_short["Overall_Rank"] > 0)
    & (df_short[["Swim", "Bike", "Run", "Finish"]] > 0).all(axis=1)
    & (~df_short["T1_Reported"] | (df_short["Transition_1"] > 0))
    & df_short["Gender"].isin(["Male", "Female"])
    & (short_diff.abs() <= 5)
)
df_short_tidy = df_short.loc[short_valid].drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

df_new_tidy = pd.concat([df_short_tidy, df_full_tidy], ignore_index=True)

print("Full-distance records:     ", len(df_full_raw), "raw →", len(df_full_tidy), "valid")
print("Sprint/Olympic records:    ", len(df_short_raw), "raw →", len(df_short_tidy), "valid")
print("Total cleaned new records:", len(df_new_tidy))
print("Valid results by distance:")
display(df_new_tidy["Race_Distance"].value_counts().to_frame("Results"))
print("Records by year and distance:")
display(pd.crosstab(df_new_tidy["Year"], df_new_tidy["Race_Distance"]))

# Quality-control summary: we check how many records were retained per selected edition
clean_counts = df_new_tidy.groupby(["Source_File", "Event", "Race_Date"]).size().rename("Valid_Results")

# the selected file paths include the repository root, so we use relative paths to match our cleaned tables
selection = df_catalog[
    df_catalog["File"].isin([str(file) for file, _ in selected_files])
].copy()
raw_counts = selection[["File", "Event", "Race_Date", "Results"]].copy()
raw_counts = raw_counts.rename(columns={"Results": "Raw_Results"})
raw_counts["Source_File"] = raw_counts["File"].map(
    lambda p: str(Path(p).relative_to(results_folder))
)
quality_report = raw_counts.merge(
    clean_counts.reset_index()[["Source_File", "Valid_Results"]],
    on="Source_File", how="left"
)
quality_report["Valid_Results"] = quality_report["Valid_Results"].fillna(0).astype(int)
quality_report["Excluded"] = quality_report["Raw_Results"] - quality_report["Valid_Results"]

This table lets us inspect the cleaning process for each original TSV file. Raw_Results is the number of rows originally loaded, Valid_Results is the number passing our filters, and Excluded is the difference. Source_File makes it possible to trace each count back to its race edition and distance.


A larger excluded count does not tell us by itself why those records were excluded. They may have incomplete results, invalid times, a missing or invalid rank, or another failed check.






















2.6 Tidy Data and Limitations¶
The cleaned tables follow tidy data principles: each row represents one athlete's result in one race edition, with separate columns for split times, gender, age, and event information. All time measurements are in seconds.


We prefer to preserve uncertainty but not guess missing values. In particular:


    

  • T1/T2: Some shorter race files do not report transitions separately, so they remain missing. Sometimes their recorded sport splits may include transition time, and this limits their exact comparability with IRONMAN split times.
    • 

  • Professional status: The selected Japanese events do not consistently identify professionals, so Is_Pro remains unknown (not False).
    • 

  • Age: Japanese events provide numeric ages, but the IRONMAN sources usually provide age bands. We retain the original age categories when available and create standardized five-year age bands for comparison.
    • 

  • Coverage: Selected races and years are not randomly sampled, and the same athlete may appear in different race editions. These factors must be considered in later analysis.
    • 























3. Harmonize Dataset 1 and Dataset 2¶






















We retained both datasets separately, but we are going to create now a common set of columns so that results can also be analyzed together. We will not use merge() to match athletes because the datasets do not share a reliable athlete identifier as index. We need to use pd.concat() then and keep a race-distance and data-source label for each observation.


















In [ ]:






# we prepare our original IRONMAN 70.3 results using the same variable names
df_half = df_tidy.copy()
df_half["Race_Distance"] = "IRONMAN 70.3"
df_half["Race_Date"] = pd.NA  # Dataset 1 only reports the race year
df_half["Source_File"] = pd.NA
df_half["Data_Source"] = "IRONMAN 70.3 (Kaggle)"
df_half["Age_Exact"] = np.nan  # Exact ages are not available in Dataset 1
df_half["Age_Estimate"] = df_half["Age_Group_Mean"]
df_half["Competition_Group"] = df_half["Is_Pro"].map({True: "Professional", False: "Age-group"})
df_half["Timing_Convention"] = "Five splits reported separately"

# we select shared variables in the same order from both datasets
common_cols = [
    "Event", "Year", "Race_Date", "Race_Distance", "Gender",
    "Age_Group", "Age_Exact", "Age_Estimate", "Is_Pro", "Competition_Group",
    "Swim", "Transition_1", "Bike", "Transition_2", "Run", "Finish",
    "Data_Source", "Source_File", "Timing_Convention"
]

df_combined = pd.concat([
    df_half.reindex(columns=common_cols),
    df_new_tidy.reindex(columns=common_cols)
], ignore_index=True)

print("Combined observations:", len(df_combined))
display(df_combined["Race_Distance"].value_counts())
display(df_combined.head())

df_combined contains one row per athlete race result, with the same column names for all four distance categories. Race_Distance and Data_Source identify where each result belongs, while Timing_Convention records important differences in how splits were reported to account for possible misleading calculations.


The missing values are not all data errors. For example, Dataset 1 does not contain exact ages or race dates, and some Japanese editions do not have separately reported transitions or professional status. We decided to keep those fields missing istead of filling them with unsupported values.






















3.1 Subset for Race Distances Comparisons¶
The two datasets cover different years. For comparisons within the four distances during overlapping years, we create a subset for 2017 and 2019. We also calculate swimming and running percentile ranks within each race, year, distance, and gender (which allows us to compare an athlete's relative performances without directly comparing raw split durations from different race distances). The absolute difference between the two percentiles, Balance_Gap, is one possible measure of relative balance


















In [ ]:






# within-race percentile rankings (lower values are faster split times)
groups = ["Data_Source", "Race_Distance", "Event", "Year", "Gender"]
df_combined["Swim_Percentile"] = df_combined.groupby(groups)["Swim"].rank(pct=True)
df_combined["Run_Percentile"] = df_combined.groupby(groups)["Run"].rank(pct=True)
df_combined["Balance_Gap"] = (
    df_combined["Swim_Percentile"] - df_combined["Run_Percentile"]
).abs()

df_overlap_years = df_combined[df_combined["Year"].isin([2017, 2019])].copy()

print("All four distances (whole sample):")
display(df_combined["Race_Distance"].value_counts())

print("Results in the overlapping years (2017 and 2019):")
display(df_overlap_years["Race_Distance"].value_counts())

The combined dataset contains 869,989 observations from the four triathlon distances. IRONMAN 70.3 accounts for the majority of the data (840,057 observations), followed by Full IRONMAN (22,691), Olympic (5,961), and Sprint (1,280).


When restricting the analysis to the overlapping years (2017 and 2019), we retain 237,913 observations across all four distances. This allows us to compare swimming and running performance over the same time period, which we believe is important for reducing potential differences that are associated with changes across years.


Although sample sizes remain considerably different, especially because Dataset 1, IRONMAN 70.3, covers many more competitions than Dataset 2. When comparing correlations and performance balance across distances, we will analyze each distance separately and we will also have to account for differences in their size and race characteristics.






















3.2 Gender-Based Datasets¶
Finally, we split our data into two datasets, one for female and one for male athletes. Gender plays a big role in performance so we want to compare seperately in women and men.

4. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶






















Our EDA is split into two sections, one for our first dataset and one for our combined data after extracting from both datasets. We first consider the summary statistics in the Ironman 70.3 races using df_tidy. We then move on to Combined Summary Statistics where we are equiped with df_combined and df_overlap_years. We will use the first for our general correlation statistics, and the second for exploring balance.






















4.1. Summary Statistics Ironman 70.3¶
    

  • Number of results by gender: To understand the composition of our dataset.
    • 

  • Median swimming and running times by gender: To compare typical performance across groups.
    • 

  • Overall Pearson correlation: To measure the strength of the linear relationship between swimming and running times.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation by gender: To investigate whether this relationship differs between male and female athletes.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation for professional athletes: To examize whether the relationship changes for male and female professional athletes.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation by age group: To explore whether the relationship varies across age categories.
    • 























For this part of the analysis we use df_tidy. This is the part of the EDA from Milestone 1. We explore the correlation in the results from Ironman 70.3 specifically.


















In [ ]:






print("Results by gender:")
print(df_tidy["Gender"].value_counts())

print("\nMedian swimming and running times (minutes):")
median_times = df_tidy.groupby("Gender")[["Swim", "Run"]].median() / 60 # Median times by gender, converted to minutes
display(median_times.round(2))

print("\nOverall Pearson correlation:")
pearson = df_tidy["Swim"].corr(df_tidy["Run"])
print("Pearson correlation:", round(pearson, 3)) # Overall swimming-running correlation

print("\nPearson correlation by gender:") # Correlation by gender
for gender, group in df_tidy.groupby("Gender"):
    correlation = group["Swim"].corr(group["Run"], method="pearson")
    print(gender, round(correlation, 3))

Swimming vs. Running by Gender:¶


















In [ ]:






plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))

for gender, color in [("Female", "tab:blue"), ("Male", "tab:orange")]:

    group = df_tidy[df_tidy["Gender"] == gender]

    correlation = group["Swim"].corr(group["Run"]) # This is the Pearson correlation using all observations

    sample = group.sample(n=3000, random_state=42) # We take a sample for visualization

    plt.scatter(
        sample["Swim"] / 60,
        sample["Run"] / 60,
        alpha=0.3,
        s=10,
        label=f"{gender} (r = {correlation:.3f})"
    )

    slope, intercept = np.polyfit( # We create a linear regression line using all observations
        group["Swim"] / 60,
        group["Run"] / 60,
        1
    )

    x = np.linspace(
        sample["Swim"].min() / 60,
        sample["Swim"].max() / 60,
        100
    )

    plt.plot(
        x,
        slope * x + intercept,
        color=color,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"{gender} (r = {correlation:.3f})"
    )

plt.xlabel("Swimming Time (minutes)")
plt.ylabel("Running Time (minutes)")
plt.title("Swimming vs. Running Performance by Gender")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(alpha=0.2)
plt.show()
















































Important clarification:  Since our dataset contains over 840,000 observations, we randomly selected 3,000 results per gender to avoid overcrowding the scatter plot. However, the Pearson correlations were calculated using the full dataset to preserve the accuracy of our analysis.






















With this scatter plot we can visualize the relationship between swimming and running times for male and female competitors. The regression line shows a positive linear trend, which suggests that slower swimmers tend to have slower running times. However, there is a considerable spread of observations, so we cannot explain running performance based on swimming performance alone or vice versa.

We can see how the Pearson correlation between swimming and running times generally decreases across older age groups, from approximately 0.49 among athletes aged 30–34 to 0.27 among those aged 70–74. This suggests that the linear relationship between the two disciplines may be weaker in older age groups. But we will need to investigate other attribute differences such as sample size, competitive level, and race conditions that could also contribute to this pattern.






















4.2 Combined Summary Statistics¶
    

  • Number of results by gender: To understand the composition of our dataset.
    • 

  • Median swimming and running times by gender: To compare typical performance across groups.
    • 

  • Overall Pearson Pooled Correlation: To measure the strength of the linear relationship between swimming and running times in a larger model including different races.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation by race distance and gender: To investigate whether this relationship differs between male and female athletes, in different triathlon distances, Sprint, Olympic, Ironman 70.3, Full Ironman.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation for professional athletes and by race distance: To examize whether the relationship changes for male and female professional athletes and between race distances.
    • 

  • Pearson correlation by age group and race distance: To explore whether the relationship varies across age categories and according to each race distance.
    • 

  • Swimming-Running Performance Balance by race distance: To investigate whether triathletes tend to be balanced in their swimming and running based on their percentile.
    • 

  • Percentages of relatively balanced athletes by gender: To measure how many triathletes are balanced in their swimming and running.
    • 























In this first part we use df_combined to calculate Pearson correlation. However, we notice a big change in our correlation compared to the previous results. We understand that calculating Pearson correlation using our df_combined dataset would be misleading, since it combines four different races. These races have different distances and consequently different swimming and running times. The overall correlation may capture not only the relationship between swimming and running performance within individual race distances, but also the differences in performance times between race distances. For example, a full Ironman has longer swimming and running times, which can increase the overall correlation. Following, we have presented how this works in our dataset.


We will keep this Pooled correlation in our analysis to demonstrate how a calculation like this may be misleading. However, we clarify that the Overall Pooled correlation will not be used as our main correlation since it does not accurately count for different race distances.

Swimming-Running Performance Balance¶






















To analyze if athletes exhibit more balanced swimming and running times for different triathlon distances, we use our Balance_Gap variable created during the ETL process. Since Sprint, Olympic, IRONMAN 70.3, and Full IRONMAN races involve different swimming and running distances, comparing just times would not provide meaningful information about balance. Instead, we need to use percentile rankings to evaluate each triathlete's swimming and running performance compared with other athletes in the same race and gender group.


The Swim_Percentile and Run_Percentile variables represent an athlete's relative ranking in swimming and running. If theBalance_Gap is small, we understand that the athlete performs similarly in swimming an running, while if the gap is large we understand that the athlete performs relatively better in one discipline than the other. For example, an athlete in the 20th percentile for swimming and the 25th percentile for running has a Balance Gap of 0.05, which shows us balance. In contrast, an athlete in the 10th percentile for swimming and the 80th percentile for running has a Balance Gap of 0.70, meaning that they are much better in swimming than in running. Something to point out is that a small Balance_Gap doesn't necessarily mean great performance overall, it only measures similarity.


We will use df_overlap_years, that has races in 2017 and 2019, to make the results more consistent. However, differences in race locations, course conditions, like weather, and number of athletes may still influence the results.

Relatively Balanced Athletes¶






















We introduce a new measure for a triathlete being balanced For our analysis, we will consider triathletes with a Balance_Gap less than 0.1 to be relatively balanced triathletes. This means that their relative swimming and running performance is similar. We want to calculate the percentage of the total athletes per race distance that are relatively balanced athletes. We point out that 0.1 is our choice based on the previous results and how we view the sports as athletes.

Conclusion¶
Overall, our analysis shows a positive correlation between swimming and running across all four race distances. Fast swimmers tend to be fast runners. The relationship slightly varies throughout different races, while it seems to weaken with increasing age. When investigating swimming and running balance, we found that Balance Gaps are similar across all race distances and specifically shorter races appear to have slightly smaller median Balance Gaps. The percentages of relatively balanced athletes remain around 30-35% in all race distances and both genders.






















5. Proposed Models¶






















From our findings, we will focus our approach on developing two models to answer our research questions. The first will investigate the relationship between swimming and running performance and whether it changes depending on race distance and athlete characteristics. The second will study race distances and other characteristics and their association with more balanced swimming and running performances.


For our main comparisons, we will use df_overlap_years, which contains results from 2017 and 2019 across all four distances. We will also repeat important parts of the analysis using df_combined to see if including the remaining years changes our conclusions.






















5.1 Model 1: Predicting Running Performance and Comparing Swimming-Running Relationships¶
Research Question: Does swimming performance predict running performance, and does this relationship differ depending on race distance, gender, age, and competitive status?


This model is intended to address our first three research questions.


Motivation from our EDA: Our EDA showed positive Pearson correlations between swimming and running times for all four distances:






Race Distance
Pearson Correlation (r)






Full IRONMAN
0.529




IRONMAN 70.3
0.491




Olympic
0.453




Sprint
0.519






These correlations suggest that athletes with faster swimming times generally also tend to have faster running times. But we can also see how the relationship is not equally strong across distances.
We have also observed differences when separating athletes by gender, age group, and competitive status. For example, the correlation among professional female athletes was 0.186 in Full IRONMAN, compared with 0.551 among professional male athletes. The corresponding correlations among amateur athletes were considerably closer (0.508 for women and 0.497 for men).
We also noticed that correlations generally decreased across older age groups. These results made us ask ourselves an important question: are the differences we observe still present when we consider several athlete characteristics at the same time?






















Proposed Method: Multiple Linear Regression with Interaction Terms


We plan to use multiple linear regression to examine how swimming performance is associated with running performance while accounting for other variables.
A simple linear regression could predict running time using swimming time alone. However, this would not allow us to study the relationship and if it differs between Sprint, Olympic, IRONMAN 70.3, and Full IRONMAN events.
For this reason, we propose including interaction terms between swimming performance and race distance.
An interaction term allows the relationship between swimming and running to have a different slope for each race distance, so we don’t assume that the same relationship applies to every triathlon format.
We could also include an interaction between swimming performance and gender to study how the relationship also differs between male and female athletes.






















Variables:


Dependent Variable (Y):


    

  • Standardized Running Time: Running performance relative to other athletes competing in the same race edition.
    • 



Independent Variables (X):


    

  • Standardized Swimming Time: Swimming performance
    

    • 

  • Race_Distance: Sprint, Olympic, IRONMAN 70.3, or Full IRONMAN.
    

    • 

  • Gender: Male or Female.
    

    • 

  • Age: Athlete age or an estimated age based on the available age group.
    

    • 

  • Swimming Performance x Race Distance: An interaction term that allows the swimming-running relationship to vary by distance
    

    • 

  • Swimming Performance x Gender: An interaction term that allows the relationship to vary by gender
    

    • 



We could also investigate Is_Pro in a separate analysis restricted to IRONMAN 70.3 and Full IRONMAN, where professional status is available.






















Hypotheses


    

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): After accounting for the included athlete characteristics, the relationship between standardized swimming and running times does not differ across race distances.
    

    • 

  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): The relationship between standardized swimming and running times differs for at least one race distance.
    

    • 



We could also investigate additional hypotheses about whether the relationship changes by gender or competitive status.






















5.2 Model 2: Investigating Swimming-Running Performance Balance Across Race Distances¶
Research Question: Do athletes tend to exhibit more balanced swimming and running performances in shorter or longer triathlon events?


This model focuses on our fourth research question.


Motivation from our EDA: To compare swimming and running performance across different race distances, we created three variables during ETL:


Swim_Percentile: An athlete's relative swimming ranking within the same race edition and gender group.


Run_Percentile: An athlete's relative running ranking within the same race edition and gender group.


Balance_Gap: The absolute difference between the swimming and running percentile rankings.


A smaller Balance Gap means that an athlete has more similar relative performances in swimming and running.
For example, an athlete ranked in the 20th percentile for swimming and the 25th percentile for running would have a Balance Gap of 0.05, while an athlete ranked in the 10th percentile for swimming and the 80th percentile for running would have a Balance Gap of 0.70.


But a smaller Balance Gap does not necessarily mean that an athlete is highly competitive in both disciplines. It only measures how similar their relative rankings are.


Our EDA produced the following median Balance Gaps using df_overlap_years:

The Balance Gap is very close for all four distances. Even though sprint distances have the smallest median gap, the difference is not large.


We also examined the percentage of athletes with a Balance Gap less than 0.1, naming them relatively balanced athletes. Approximately 30-35% of athletes met this criterion across all race distances and genders.


These findings suggest that performance balance is relatively consistent across triathlon distances, but we do not yet know if the small differences we observe are statistically meaningful.






















Proposed Method: Quantile Regression (focused on the Median)


We propose Quantile Regression, focusing on the median, to study swimminf and running performance balance and if it differs across race distances and gender.


We chose this approach because Balance Gap is a nonnegative variable ranging from 0 to 1, and its distribution does not necessarily follow a normal distribution.


In our EDA, we focused on the median since it is less affected by extremely large or small values rather than the mean. That is why median regression would allow us to continue analyzing the median, while considering several variables.






















Variables


Dependent Variable (Y):


    

  • Balance_Gap: The absolute difference between Swim_Percentile and Run_Percentile.
    • 



Independent Variables (X):


    

  • Race_Distance: Sprint, Olympic, IRONMAN 70.3, or Full IRONMAN.
    

    • 

  • Gender: Male or Female.
    

    • 

  • Age: Athlete age or estimated age group.
    

    • 

  • Year: Competition year, to account for possible differences over time.
    

    • 



We would not initially include professional status in the model across all four distances because this information is not reliably available for Sprint and Olympic events. If needed, we would perform an additional analysis restricted to the Ironman 70.3 and Full Ironman that are equiped with the professional status of each athlete.






















Hypotheses


    

  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): The median Balance Gap does not differ across race distances after accounting for the included athlete characteristics.
    

    • 

  • Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): At least one race distance is associated with a different median Balance Gap.
    

    • 



We are interested in whether shorter events tend to have smaller Balance Gaps, but we will not assume that this pattern exists before testing it.






















6. Limitations and Next Steps¶
    

  • Standarizing times: One of the main challenges is that the race distances are very different.
    

    For example, swimming 750 meters in a Sprint triathlon takes much less time than swimming 3.8 kilometers in a Full IRONMAN. So we can't directly compare those times as if they represented the same physical task. Also, even races of the same distance may differ in course conditions, elevation, currents, or weather.
    

    To make the measurements more comparable, we plan to standardize swimming and running times within each race edition using z-scores. We will then use these standardized values in our regression (not pooling raw times from races).
    

    This should reduce the influence of differences in average race times, although it will not completely eliminate differences in course difficulty or athlete populations.
    

    • 

  • Differences Between Competittions: Race and course conditions may affect swimming and running times even when distances are identical.
    

    For example, bad weather can make the swimming course larger by moving the buoys further from each other, affect body temperature for athletes, and make running harder against wind. These changes in each event cannot always be known, however, by standarizing times we can make comparisons more meaningful.
    

    • 

  • Missing Athlete Information: Professional status is not included in most Sprint and Olympic results, and exact ages are not consistently reported across the two datasets.
    

    We will avoid using professional status when it is unknown for our athletes and use the age inofrmation with some limitations and caution.
    

    • 

  • Differences in Timing Conventions: As already mentioned in the ETL, some Japanese sprint and Olympic race files did not report transition times separately, rather had them as part of the swimming, bikinf or running times. As a result, some swimming or running splits might not be directly equivalent to the swimming and runnng splits in the first data set of Ironman 70.3.
    

    We will preserve the original timing information and discuss this limitation when interpreting differences across distances.
    

    •
